_note: Drafts written by the engineer for Neha and Achal to edit and Aseem to ratify (N1). `words` is what the prompt reads; `check` is what the verifier enforces. Digits are [top, bottom]. regroups lists the allowed counts.

skill_sets.name: 2-digit addition with regrouping
skill_sets.learning_objective: Adds two numbers by columns, making a new ten (or hundred) exactly when a column total reaches ten.

Easy.words: A 2-digit number plus a 1-digit number, with one regroup in the ones. Total under 100.

Medium.words: Two 2-digit numbers with one regroup in the ones. Total under 100.

Hard.words: Two 2-digit numbers with two regroups, ones and tens, so the total passes 100.

Advance.words: A 3-digit number plus a 2-digit number with one or two regroups. The child must line up the shorter number.

skill_sets.name: 2-digit subtraction with exchange
skill_sets.learning_objective: Subtracts by columns, exchanging one ten for ten ones exactly when the ones column needs it.
philosophy: The larger number is always on top. Never write a subtraction the child cannot do.

Easy.words: A 2-digit number minus a 1-digit number, with one exchange.

Medium.words: A 2-digit number minus a 2-digit number, with one exchange.

Hard.words: A 3-digit number minus a 2-digit number, with one exchange. The child must line up the shorter number.

Advance.words: A 3-digit number minus a 3-digit number, with one or two exchanges. No zero anywhere in the top number.

skill_sets.name: 3-digit addition with regrouping
skill_sets.learning_objective: Adds 3-digit numbers by columns with one or more regroups, carrying into the correct column each time.

Easy.words: A 3-digit number plus a 2-digit number with one regroup.

Advance.words: A 4-digit number plus a 3-digit number with two or three regroups.

skill_sets.name: 3-digit subtraction across zero
skill_sets.learning_objective: Exchanges across a zero: takes a hundred, turns the zero into nine tens and ten ones, and keeps every column's value right.
philosophy: The larger number is always on top.

Easy.words: Two 3-digit numbers with one exchange and no zero in the top number. A warm-up before zeros.

Medium.words: Two 3-digit numbers where the top number has a zero in the tens, and the child must exchange across it.

Hard.words: Two 3-digit numbers across a zero, with two exchanges.

Advance.words: Two 4-digit numbers across zeros, with two or three exchanges.

skill_sets.name: Addition within 10
skill_sets.learning_objective: Combines two small sets into a total of 10 or less, and reads + as 'combine' and = as 'is the same as', not 'the answer comes next'.
philosophy: No column layout at this rung — one line, both numbers, the + and = signs printed exactly as the child should read them.

Easy.words: Two numbers that combine to 5 or less, e.g. 2 + 3.

Medium.words: Two numbers that combine to 10 or less, written as a sum.

Hard.words: The same sums within 10, but told as a short story the child must read first.

Advance.words: A missing addend within 10, written a + □ = c, so = is read as balance rather than 'next comes the answer'.

skill_sets.name: Addition within 20, crossing ten
skill_sets.learning_objective: Adds two numbers whose total passes 10 by using ten as a landmark (make-ten / part-part-whole), and applies the +1 and +10 patterns without recomputing from one.

Easy.words: A 1-digit number plus a 1-digit number that together cross 10, e.g. 8 + 5.

Medium.words: A teen number (11-19) plus a 1-digit number, written as a sum.

Hard.words: The same teen-plus-ones sums, told as a short story the child must read first.

Advance.words: The number-line format: the child names the landing point after a jump to the nearest ten, then the total.

skill_sets.name: Subtraction within 20
skill_sets.learning_objective: Subtracts within 20 both as take-away (how many are left) and as comparison (how many more), and connects the two to the same fact family.
philosophy: The larger number is always on top.

Easy.words: A number to 10 minus a 1-digit number, take-away only.

Medium.words: A teen number minus a 1-digit number, crossing back through 10.

Hard.words: A comparison ('how many more') word problem within 20, where the operation is not named in the stem.

Advance.words: A missing-number form, □ − b = c or c − □ = a, within 20.

skill_sets.name: 2-digit addition and subtraction without regrouping
skill_sets.learning_objective: Adds and subtracts two 2-digit numbers by columns, ones under ones and tens under tens, with no exchange needed in either column.
philosophy: The larger number is always on top for subtraction.
Mix addition and subtraction items evenly within a set; never block all of one operation together.

Easy.words: A 2-digit number plus or minus a 1-digit number, no regroup.

Medium.words: Two 2-digit numbers, no regroup needed in either column.

Hard.words: Two 2-digit numbers, no regroup, written horizontally so the child must convert to columns correctly before calculating.

Advance.words: A 2-digit number and a 1-digit number, no regroup, with the shorter number written first — order must not change the column alignment.

skill_sets.name: Mental strategies: bridging, friendly numbers, equality
skill_sets.learning_objective: Solves without a written column algorithm — bridging through ten, using a friendly (round) number, or reasoning about what balances an equation — and reads = as balance, not 'the answer comes next'.
philosophy: No column grid is offered at this rung; the format itself forces a mental or jotted strategy rather than a rule about it.

Code verifies the numeric answer in every format here (missing_number / balance_scale / number_wall each carry a computed correct answer and misconception table). Whether the child actually bridged or reasoned about balance, rather than counted on by ones, is not a gradable claim code can check — no verifier is invented for it. A future 'show your jump' claim would route through validate_item's per-template check and its ≤5% item sample, per ADR 0009 and ADR 0010, never a per-item model call.

Easy.words: A missing addend within 20, found by bridging through ten rather than counting on by ones.

Medium.words: A missing part in a subtraction fact within 50, using a friendly-number jump.

Hard.words: A balance equation, a + b = □ + c, in tens to 150 — the child finds the missing number without adding both sides out in full.

Advance.words: A number wall: each brick is the sum of the two below it, within 100, solved without writing every column sum out in full.

skill_sets.name: One- and two-step word problems
skill_sets.learning_objective: Reads a short word problem in rupees or everyday objects, picks the right operation(s) from the situation rather than a keyword, and — for two-step problems — uses the first answer inside the second step.
philosophy: Word problems use things a child in Pune knows: mangoes, rupees, cricket runs, school steps, the mela, the bus.
One short plain sentence, both numbers in it, one question at the end.

Easy.words: A one-step join or take-away story within 100, no regroup.

Medium.words: A one-step story within 100 with one regroup, where the operation is not signalled by a keyword.

Hard.words: A two-step story (money spent twice, or people getting on and off a bus), 2-digit numbers.

Advance.words: A two-step story with 3-digit numbers, and one extra number in the stem that is not needed for the answer.

skill_sets.name: Estimate first, then check reasonableness
skill_sets.learning_objective: Rounds both numbers to the nearest ten before calculating, writes a sensible estimate, then works out the exact answer and checks it is close to the estimate.
philosophy: Round to the nearest ten only at this rung — nearest hundred is R13's estimate-for-efficiency case, not this one.

Code checks the exact answer exactly and the estimate within its tolerance (both are closed digit responses). Whether the child's rounding reasoning is sound, rather than a lucky guess inside the tolerance band, is not separately scored and no verifier is invented for it — a sampled read by validate_item is the check, per ADR 0009.

Easy.words: Two 2-digit numbers, addition, one regroup. The estimate is accepted within 10 of the rounded total.

Hard.words: Two 3-digit numbers, either operation, one or two regroups.

Advance.words: Two 3-digit numbers, either operation, where the child also states whether the exact answer is 'sensible' against the estimate before it is checked.

skill_sets.name: 4-digit addition with three or more addends; 4-digit subtraction across zeros
skill_sets.learning_objective: Adds three or more 4-digit numbers in a column, carrying more than 1 into a column when the total needs it, and subtracts across one or more internal zeros in a 4-digit number.
philosophy: The larger number is always on top for subtraction.

Easy.words: Three 4-digit addends, at most one column needing a carry of 2 or more.

Hard.words: Two 4-digit numbers subtracted across one internal zero.

Advance.words: Two 4-digit numbers subtracted across two zeros.

skill_sets.name: Chooses an efficient strategy under a place-value constraint
skill_sets.learning_objective: Recognises when a question is close to a friendly hundred or thousand, or has same-tens numbers, and picks compensation or a mental shortcut over the standard column method, then can name the strategy used.
philosophy: The standard column method gets the right answer but is not 'most efficient' — the rubric names this explicitly so it is not marked correct by accident.

Code verifies the numeric answer only (answer_lookup, as elsewhere). Whether the written method is genuinely the efficient one, or column arithmetic dressed up in a sentence, is a rubric judgment — 'Any compensation / friendly-number / counting-on method stated; column method is correct but not most efficient' — read by the validator at the template level and sampled at ≤5% of a unit's items, never a per-item model call. No code verifier is invented for the strategy claim, per ADR 0009.

Easy.words: A 3-digit number plus a number within 2 of 100 (e.g. 298, 199).

Medium.words: Two numbers with the same tens digit, subtracted, where counting on is faster than exchanging.

Hard.words: A 4-digit number plus a number within 2 of 1000.

Advance.words: Any of the three shortcut families, chosen at random, with the method named in one written line.

skill_sets.name: Multi-step budget word problems
skill_sets.learning_objective: Starts from a fixed budget, subtracts several costs in sequence, and reports what remains — the shape of the class-picnic problem the school actually uses.
philosophy: Word problems use things a child in Pune knows: mangoes, rupees, cricket runs, school steps, the mela, the bus.
The budget is always enough to cover every cost — never a 'not enough money' trap at this rung.

Easy.words: A budget minus two costs, values in the hundreds.

Medium.words: A budget minus three costs, values in the hundreds.

Hard.words: A budget minus three costs, values in the low thousands.

Advance.words: A budget minus four costs, one of which is itself a two-step calculation (a per-child cost times a headcount) before it is subtracted.

skill_sets.name: Multiplication by a single digit
skill_sets.learning_objective: Multiplies a 2- or 3-digit number by a single digit, carrying into the next column when a column product passes ten.
philosophy: Never ×1 or ×10 — those test nothing.
The times tables this rung assumes are 2 to 9; a child who does not have them yet belongs on a counting rung, not here.

Easy.words: A 2-digit number times a single digit, product under 100 — no carry into the tens.

Medium.words: A 2-digit number times a single digit, product past 100.

Hard.words: A 3-digit number times a single digit.

skill_sets.name: Explains the procedure or judges a claim
skill_sets.learning_objective: Given a claim about a shortcut (e.g. moving 1 between two numbers keeps the total the same), decides if it is true and explains why in the child's own words.
philosophy: Accept any explanation that shows the underlying reasoning, not a fixed sentence — Neha and Achal own the rubric wording.

There is no numeric answer to verify by code here: the response is a tick (true/false) plus free text. The tick is checkable against the planted claim's known truth value; the explanation's quality is judged only by the rubric, read by the validator at the template level and sampled at ≤5% of items, per ADR 0009 and ADR 0010. No per-item code verifier is invented for the explanation.

Easy.words: A compensation claim about two 2-digit numbers (e.g. 47 + 38 gives the same total as 46 + 39).

Medium.words: The same claim shape with a 3-digit number and a near-hundred number.

Hard.words: A claim that is false, so the child must catch the flaw rather than just agree.

Advance.words: A claim about exchange/regrouping itself (e.g. 'trading a ten for ten ones changes the total') rather than about compensation.

skill_sets.name: Finds the mistake in a worked example
skill_sets.learning_objective: Reads a worked column calculation with one planted, named misconception, locates which column the mistake is in, and writes the correct answer.
philosophy: Plant exactly one misconception per item, drawn from the vocabulary already in `misconception`, never an invented error.

Code verifies the planted mistake's arithmetic (the wrong answer shown is computed by the same predictor the misconception vocabulary uses) and the tick for 'where'. The free-text 'why' line is judged by the rubric named in the item, read by the validator at the template level and sampled at ≤5% of items — no per-item code verifier for the written explanation, per ADR 0009 and ADR 0010.

Easy.words: A 2-digit addition with a forgotten-carry mistake planted.

Medium.words: A 2-digit addition or subtraction with one of the two named column mistakes planted.

Hard.words: A 3-digit calculation with the mistake planted in a column that is not the ones column, so the child cannot default to 'always the first column'.

Advance.words: The child also writes, in one line, what the person did wrong — not just where.
